sounds.name: Four-Note Brass
sounds.ref: In the style of early-80s synth-pop brass stabs
sounds.blurb: Bright sawtooth chords that bloom open on every stab.
sounds.how: In POLY each key of a chord takes an oscillator of its own, so four sawtooths set the same way play four notes. All the notes go through one filter and one contour, so every stab opens and closes as a block: that shared swell is the brass sound. Chorus widens it.

steps.title: Four sawtooths, one per note
steps.why:
POLY is the Poly D’s chord mode: each key you hold is given one of the four oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone), so a four-note chord uses all of them. Because every oscillator is a note, they all need the same settings or the chord comes out uneven.
- MODE POLY: each new key takes the next oscillator in turn, and the red lamp by its RANGE knob lights. MONO would put all four on one key, so a chord would collapse to a single note.
- RANGE 8’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch. One oscillator at another footage would throw one note of every chord up or down an octave.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all four: the brightest, buzziest wave, full of harmonics, and the raw material of synth brass.
- FREQUENCY +0.1 / −0.1 / +0.1 on 2–4: a tenth of a semitone either way. Too small to sound out of tune, enough to stop the chord sounding too clean.
- Listen for: hold a four-note chord and watch four lamps light. Switch MODE to MONO and play it again: one note. Then back to POLY.

steps.title: All four on, level
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. In POLY each oscillator is a note, so these knobs are really the balance between the notes of a chord.
- OSC 1–4 on: in POLY a key that lands on a switched-off oscillator plays nothing, so one note in four would go missing.
- VOLUME 6 on all four: equal levels, so every note of the chord is as loud as the others and none sticks out. Turned up together, the four drive the filter harder and the tone thickens and roughens.
- Listen for: switch OSC 4 off and play a four-note chord. One of its notes goes missing. Switch it back on.

steps.title: A darker filter that swells
steps.why:
The filter takes brightness away, and its contour (Moog’s word for envelope, a shape that runs each time you play) opens it on each stab. It is a Moog-style ladder filter in low-pass mode: lows pass, highs are cut. There is one filter for all four notes, so the whole chord opens as a block.
- CUTOFF −1.5 (about 220 Hz): mellow between stabs, with most of the buzz rolled off.
- EMPHASIS 1.5: Moog’s name for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Just a hint of edge as the filter moves.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 5: how far the contour lifts the cutoff. Sets how bright the peak of each stab gets.
- ATTACK 1.6 (about 70 ms): the filter takes a moment to open, like a brass player blowing harder at the start of a note. At 0 it is a hard stab; at 3 a slow swell.
- DECAY 680 ms, SUSTAIN 4.5: after the peak it settles about halfway, so held chords stay fairly bright.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 on: a third of key tracking, so high chords are not duller than low ones.
- Listen for: the “bwah” at the front of each chord. Sweep ATTACK between 0 and 3 to hear stab turn into swell.

steps.title: Stab-shaped loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume of each chord, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. Like the filter contour, it is shared by all four notes.
- ATTACK 0.6 (5 ms): almost instant, just soft enough to avoid a click. The swell comes from the filter, not from the volume.
- SUSTAIN 9: held chords stay at nearly full level.
- DECAY 350 ms with the DECAY switch on: there is no release knob, so this switch makes DECAY the fade after you let go. A short fade keeps stabs separate.
- Listen for: the gap between stabs. Switch DECAY off and chords stop dead on release; back on, they tail off briefly.

steps.title: Chorus for width
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in slightly delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down. It thickens the chord and is what makes the Poly D stereo: without it both outputs carry the same sound.
- Chorus ON: puts the chorus in the signal path, after the distortion.
- CHORUS I: the slow, gentle setting. It widens the chord without an obvious wobble. II alone is faster and deeper; I and II together a quick shimmer.
- Listen for: on headphones, the stabs spread out from the centre. Switch the chorus off and on to hear the chord narrow and flatten, then widen again.

sounds.name: Four-Saw Unison Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of 90s rave and big-room synth bass
sounds.blurb: Four detuned sawtooths on one note: a wide, heavy bass.
sounds.how: UNI puts all four oscillators on the one key you play. Each is tuned a little apart with its FREQUENCY knob, so they drift in and out of phase and the note sounds huge. Oscillator 4 goes an octave down for weight, and a fast filter contour gives each note a punch.

steps.title: All four on one key
steps.why:
UNI (unison) shares the four oscillators among the keys you hold. A bass line is one key at a time, so every note gets all four stacked on it, which is what makes it big.
- MODE UNI: hold one key and all four OSCILLATOR lamps light. Hold two keys and they split two and two, so each note gets thinner. In POLY each bass note would be one thin sawtooth.
- Listen for: hold a low note. The four oscillators are still identical, so it only sounds like one louder sawtooth. The next step pulls them apart.

steps.title: Detuned sawtooths, one an octave down
steps.why:
The oscillators are tuned slightly apart so they drift in and out of phase, and the fourth drops an octave for weight. This is the classic detuned rave bass stack.
- RANGE 16’ on 1–3: footage comes from organ pipes; 16’ is an octave below normal 8’ pitch, bass territory.
- RANGE 32’ on osc 4: another octave down. The sub layer you feel on a big system.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all four: the buzziest wave, with every harmonic, so the stack has plenty of bite for the filter to shape.
- FREQUENCY +0.2 / −0.1 / +0.1 on 2–4: small, different offsets, so each pair beats at a different speed and the note sounds wide rather than simply out of tune. Past about 0.3 it starts to sound sour.
- Listen for: hold a low note and hear the slow churning. Set osc 2 FREQUENCY to 0 and the width shrinks; put it back.

steps.title: Mix
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator goes into the filter. Here the three 16’ saws lead and the sub sits a little under them.
- OSC 1–4 on: all four needed for the full stack.
- VOLUME 7 / 7 / 7 / 6: the 16’ saws carry the tone, and the 32’ sub at 6 adds weight without swamping the note. Levels this high push the filter a little harder, which thickens the sound.
- Listen for: turn osc 4 VOLUME down to 0 and back up to 6 while holding a note. The bottom octave falls away and returns.

steps.title: Punchy filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Here it sits low and its contour (Moog’s word for envelope) flicks it open on each note, which gives every note a punch.
- CUTOFF −2 (about 160 Hz): dark at rest, so the stack is mostly weight between hits.
- EMPHASIS 2.5: Moog’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A little edge on the snap; at 6 it turns into a squelch.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 5: how far each note lifts the cutoff. More is a harder hit.
- DECAY 310 ms, SUSTAIN 2.5: with ATTACK at 0 (1 ms) it opens at once, falls back in about a third of a second and settles low, so the punch is at the front.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 on: a third of key tracking, so higher notes in the riff are a little brighter.
- Listen for: a “dow” at the start of each note. Sweep DECAY while the riff plays to hear it tighten and loosen.

steps.title: Tight loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes volume over time, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. For a bass line you want notes that hit at once and stop clean.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): full level instantly, lined up with the filter snap.
- SUSTAIN 9: held notes keep almost all their weight.
- DECAY 250 ms with the DECAY switch on: the Poly D has no release knob, so this switch makes DECAY the fade after you let go. Short, so notes stay separate.
- Listen for: the gaps in the riff. Clean gaps keep the bass tight; raise DECAY to 5 and the notes smear into each other.

sounds.name: Chorus Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of 80s Juno-era string pads
sounds.blurb: Slow, soft chords spread wide by the chorus.
sounds.how: Four sawtooths in POLY play the chord, a low cutoff softens them and slow attack and decay make each chord swell and fade. The chorus is the sound: its swept delays turn four plain oscillators into a wide, moving pad.

steps.title: Matching sawtooths
steps.why:
POLY gives each key you hold one of the four oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone), so a four-note chord uses all of them. For the notes to match, all four need the same octave and wave.
- MODE POLY: each new key takes the next oscillator in turn, up to four at once.
- RANGE 8’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch. Any other footage would put one note of each chord in another octave.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all four: bright and full of harmonics. The classic string-pad starting point, which the filter will soften.
- FREQUENCY 0 on 2–4: exactly in tune. The chorus will supply the movement later, so no detune is needed here.
- Listen for: hold a chord. It is bright and static for now, like a plain organ.

steps.title: Mix
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator (and so each note of a chord) goes into the filter.
- OSC 1–4 on: in POLY a key that lands on a switched-off oscillator is silent, so all four must be on for full chords.
- VOLUME 5.5 on all four: a moderate, even level. Every note of the chord matches, and the filter is not driven hard, so the pad stays soft rather than gritty.
- Listen for: play a four-note chord and turn one VOLUME down to 0. One note fades out of the chord. Put it back to 5.5.

steps.title: Soft filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Here it is set low and its contour (Moog’s word for envelope) opens it only a little, and slowly, so each chord gently brightens as it swells.
- CUTOFF −1 (about 320 Hz): how soft the pad is. Low enough to take the fizz off the sawtooths.
- EMPHASIS 1: Moog’s word for resonance. Just a trace, no whistle.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 2.5: a small lift, so the change in brightness is gentle.
- ATTACK 770 ms, DECAY 1.0 s, SUSTAIN 6: the filter takes most of a second to open, then settles only a little lower.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 on: a third of key tracking, so high chords do not go dull.
- Listen for: hold a chord and hear it start dark and brighten over the first second.

steps.title: Slow swell and fade
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. A pad should fade in and fade out rather than start and stop.
- ATTACK 4.8 (740 ms): each chord swells in over most of a second. Lower it for a keyboard-like chord; raise it for a slower fade-in.
- SUSTAIN 9: held chords stay near full level.
- DECAY 1.2 s with the DECAY switch on: with the switch on, DECAY is also the fade after you let go, so chords overlap as you change them.
- Listen for: change chords and hear the old one tail away under the new one.

steps.title: Chorus I
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which thickens it and spreads it across the two outputs. On this pad the chorus is the sound: it turns four plain oscillators into a wide, moving pad.
- Chorus ON: puts the chorus in, after the distortion. With it off, both outputs carry the same sound.
- CHORUS I on, II off: I alone is a slow, gentle sweep. Pressing II as well gives a quick, shallow shimmer instead.
- Listen for: switch the chorus off and on while holding a chord. Off, the pad goes flat and narrow; on, it spreads wide and slowly moves.

sounds.name: Fuzz Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s prog-rock synth leads through a fuzz pedal
sounds.blurb: A singing mono lead with glide, driven through the distortion.
sounds.how: MONO puts every oscillator on the one note: two sawtooths and a square an octave down. Glide makes it slide between notes. The distortion after the amplifier compresses and fattens it, and the resonant filter gives it a vocal edge.

steps.title: One note, three oscillators
steps.why:
MONO puts every switched-on oscillator (the parts that make the raw tone) on the one key you press, so three of them stack into one thick lead note. The mixer sets how loud each is going into the filter.
- MODE MONO: one note at a time, all oscillators on it.
- RANGE 8’ / 8’ / 16’: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch and 16’ an octave below, for body.
- WAVEFORM saw / saw / square: two bright saws on top, and a hollow square underneath for weight.
- Osc 2 FREQUENCY +0.1: a tenth of a semitone sharp, so the two saws beat slowly and the note moves.
- OSC 1–3 on, VOLUME 7 / 6.5 / 5: OSC 4 off. The saws lead and the square sits under them.
- Listen for: hold a note and switch osc 3 off and on to hear the octave below come and go.

steps.title: Glide
steps.why:
Glide slides the pitch from one note to the next instead of jumping, the singing, sliding move of a prog lead. On the Poly D it has an on/off switch beside the keys and a time knob on the main panel.
- GLIDE switch on: without it the knob does nothing.
- GLIDE knob 3.5 (240 ms): about a quarter of a second per slide. Higher is lazier and swoopier; lower is just a quick scoop.
- Listen for: play two notes an octave apart. The pitch sweeps between them. Switch GLIDE off and it jumps.

steps.title: Resonant filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Here it sits in the middle with some emphasis, so the lead has a vocal edge, and a gentle contour (Moog’s word for envelope) brightens each note’s start.
- CUTOFF 0.2 (about 730 Hz): half open, so the saws still buzz but are not harsh.
- EMPHASIS 4: Moog’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Gives the nasal, singing edge.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 3, DECAY 770 ms: with ATTACK at 8 ms and SUSTAIN 5, a mild lift at the start of each note that settles halfway.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 and 2 on: full key tracking, so the cutoff follows the notes and high notes keep the same colour as low ones.
- Listen for: the slight “wah” at the start of each note. Sweep EMPHASIS from 0 to 6 to hear the edge grow.

steps.title: Sustained loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. A lead has to hold its level for as long as you hold the note.
- ATTACK 0.3 (2 ms): immediate start without a click.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level for as long as the key is down, so long notes sing.
- DECAY 600 ms with the DECAY switch on: the fade after you let go, since the Poly D has no separate release.
- Listen for: hold a long note. It stays at full level. Let go and it tails off over about half a second.

steps.title: Drive it
steps.why:
The distortion sits after the amplifier and before the chorus. Driving it squashes the peaks, so the lead gets louder-sounding, more sustained and fuzzier, like a synth through a guitar pedal.
- Distortion ON: puts it in the signal path.
- DIST 6: well driven. Below 3 it only thickens; above 7 it buzzes hard.
- TONE 4: a little dark, so the fuzz stays smooth rather than fizzy. Turn it right for a harsher top.
- LEVEL 3.5: turned down to keep the volume close to the clean sound, as driving it makes it louder.
- Listen for: switch the distortion off and on while holding a note. On, the note is thicker, compressed and grittier.

sounds.name: Arpeggio Chords
sounds.ref: In the style of 80s arpeggiated synth-pop
sounds.blurb: Hold a chord and the arpeggiator plays it as a bright, bouncing line.
sounds.how: ARP plays the held keys one at a time at the TEMPO rate. Each arpeggio note is a single note, so the patch is set in MONO with three oscillators stacked on it. A plucky contour makes each step distinct and the chorus spreads the line.

steps.title: A stacked single voice
steps.why:
The arpeggiator will play held chords one note at a time, so the voice only ever plays single notes. MONO stacks three oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone) on each of those notes for a full sound.
- MODE MONO: every switched-on oscillator plays the one note.
- RANGE 8’ / 4’ / 16’: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch, 4’ an octave up, 16’ an octave down. Three octaves in one note.
- WAVEFORM saw / saw / square: bright saws on top, a hollow square underneath.
- Osc 2 FREQUENCY +0.1: a hair sharp, so it beats slightly against osc 1.
- OSC 1–3 on, VOLUME 7 / 4.5 / 5: OSC 4 off. The upper octave is quietest, adding sparkle without thinning the note.
- Listen for: hold a note. Switch osc 2 off and on to hear the octave-up sparkle.

steps.title: Plucky filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. A short contour (Moog’s word for envelope) flicks it open on each note, so every arpeggio step pops.
- CUTOFF −1.2 (about 280 Hz): fairly dark between steps.
- EMPHASIS 3: Moog’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Adds a little quack to each pop.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 5.5: a big lift at the start of each note.
- ATTACK 1 ms, DECAY 280 ms, SUSTAIN 1: open at once, closed again in under a third of a second. DECAY sets how long the bright part of each step lasts.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 on: a third of key tracking, so the high notes of the arpeggio are not duller.
- Listen for: tap a note and hear a bright blip that quickly goes dark.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. Short notes keep the arpeggio steps apart.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): every step starts at once.
- DECAY 350 ms, SUSTAIN 3: the volume falls quickly to a low level, so even held notes sound plucked.
- DECAY switch on: the note also fades over 350 ms after release rather than stopping dead.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear it drop in level after the first moment.

steps.title: Start the arpeggiator
steps.why:
The arpeggiator plays the keys you hold one after another, as sixteenth notes at the TEMPO rate. Hold a chord and it becomes a bouncing line.
- ARP on: starts it. Switch it off to hear the chords themselves (as a single note in MONO).
- TEMPO 5.2 (102 BPM): the speed of the line, in sixteenth notes.
- STEP UP/DOWN: climbs through the held notes and back down. Each press of STEP moves to the next of the eight orders, shown on the LOCATION lamps.
- Listen for: hold a three- or four-note chord. The notes run up and down. Change the chord and the line follows.

steps.title: Chorus
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in slightly delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which thickens it and spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON: puts it in the signal path. Off, both outputs are the same.
- CHORUS I: the slow, gentle sweep. It widens the line without a wobble that would blur the rhythm.
- Listen for: switch the chorus off and on while the arpeggio runs. On, the line opens out to both sides.

sounds.name: One-Finger Chord Stab
sounds.ref: In the style of early Detroit techno chord stabs
sounds.blurb: A whole minor chord from one key, with a short, hollow stab.
sounds.how: In MONO all four oscillators play the key you press, so tuning them apart with their FREQUENCY knobs gives a chord on one finger: root, minor third, fifth and an octave. A short contour and a little emphasis make the stab.

steps.title: Tune the oscillators into a chord
steps.why:
MONO puts all four oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone) on the key you press, so tuning them apart turns one finger into a chord: root, minor third, fifth and octave.
- MODE MONO: every oscillator plays the one key.
- RANGE 8’ on 1–3, 4’ on osc 4: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch, 4’ an octave up for the top of the chord.
- WAVEFORM saw on 1–3, square on 4: bright chord tones with a hollower top note.
- FREQUENCY +3 on osc 2: three semitones, a minor third. At 4 the chord turns major.
- FREQUENCY +7 on osc 3: seven semitones, a fifth.
- Osc 4 FREQUENCY 0: the octave stays exact.
- Listen for: one key now plays a minor chord. Play a line and every note is its own minor chord, the Detroit stab trick.

steps.title: Mix
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator, here each note of the chord, goes into the filter.
- OSC 1–4 on: all four chord tones in.
- VOLUME 6 / 6 / 6 / 4.5: root, third and fifth even, the octave a little quieter so the top of the chord does not stick out.
- Listen for: switch OSC 2 off and on. Without the third the chord goes open and neutral; with it, it is clearly minor.

steps.title: Stab filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. A short contour (Moog’s word for envelope) opens it for an instant on each stab.
- CUTOFF −1.8 (about 180 Hz): dark at rest.
- EMPHASIS 3.5: Moog’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Gives the stab its hollow, slightly nasal ring.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 4.5, DECAY 220 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 0, a bright flash that closes fully in about a fifth of a second.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 and 2 on: full key tracking, so stabs higher up stay as bright as low ones.
- Listen for: a short “dunk” of brightness on each key. Sweep DECAY to lengthen or shorten the flash.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. For a stab, every hit should be the same short length.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant start.
- DECAY 310 ms, SUSTAIN 0: the volume falls to nothing even if the key is held, so every stab is the same length.
- DECAY switch off: letting go early cuts the note dead instead of fading.
- Listen for: hold a key and it still dies away. Short, even stabs whatever you do with your fingers.

steps.title: Chorus
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which thickens the stab and spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS I: the slow, gentle setting, for width without a wobble.
- Listen for: the stabs widen out across the speakers. Switch the chorus off to hear them snap back to the centre.

sounds.name: Rotating Oscillators
sounds.ref: The POLY mode’s oscillator rotation, used as an effect
sounds.blurb: Each new note lands on the next oscillator, so a plain line changes colour note by note.
sounds.how: In POLY every new key takes the next oscillator in turn. Set the four differently and a single-note line cycles through four timbres and pitches: here a sawtooth, a square an octave up, a triangle a fifth up and a narrow pulse. The OSCILLATOR lamps show which one each note lands on.

steps.title: Four different oscillators
steps.why:
In POLY every new key takes the next oscillator in turn, even when you play one note at a time. Set the four differently and a plain single-note line changes colour and pitch on every note.
- MODE POLY: the rotation is what makes this sound work. In MONO every note plays all four at once.
- Osc 1 RANGE 8’, sawtooth: the bright, buzzy note.
- Osc 2 RANGE 4’, square: an octave up (4’ is half the organ-pipe length of 8’), hollow.
- Osc 3 RANGE 8’, triangle, FREQUENCY +7: soft, and a fifth above what you play.
- Osc 4 RANGE 8’, narrow pulse: thin and nasal.
- FREQUENCY 0 on osc 2 and 4: in tune with the key.
- Listen for: play one key over and over and watch the four OSCILLATOR lamps take turns. Every fourth note jumps up a fifth.

steps.title: All four on
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator goes into the filter. In POLY a key that lands on a switched-off oscillator plays nothing, so all four must be on.
- OSC 1–4 on: switch OSC 2 off and every note that lands on it goes silent, leaving gaps in the line.
- VOLUME 6.5 / 5 / 7.5 / 6: balanced by ear. The square is turned down because it is loud, and the triangle up because it is quiet.
- Listen for: repeat one key. The four notes should be about equally loud even though they sound different.

steps.title: Plucky filter and loudness
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. The filter and loudness contours (Moog’s word for envelopes) are both short, so each note is a separate blip.
- CUTOFF −0.6 (about 420 Hz), EMPHASIS 3: fairly dark, with a little resonance (Moog calls it emphasis) for bite.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 4, DECAY 280 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 1.5, a quick bright pop at the start of each note.
- Loudness DECAY 310 ms, SUSTAIN 2: with ATTACK at 1 ms, each note drops fast to a low level.
- DECAY switch on: notes fade briefly on release instead of stopping dead.
- Listen for: a line of short blips, each a different colour. Raise loudness SUSTAIN to hear them run together.

steps.title: Chorus
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which widens it and spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS I: the slow, gentle sweep, for width without blurring the individual blips.
- Listen for: the line spreads out across the stereo field. Switch the chorus off and it sits in the middle again.

sounds.name: Pink Noise Surf
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s film and TV atmospheres
sounds.blurb: No oscillators at all: filtered pink noise that swells like waves.
sounds.how: Noise contains every frequency at once, and a resonant filter picks out a band of it. Long attack and decay make each held note swell and break like a wave, and the chorus spreads it across the two outputs.

steps.title: Noise only
steps.why:
No oscillators at all: the whole sound is noise, which contains every frequency at once. The filter will later pick a band out of it. Pink noise is the natural starting point for surf and wind.
- OSC 1–4 off: none of the tone-makers reaches the filter.
- Noise ON, NOISE VOLUME 8: plenty of noise into the filter.
- Noise WHITE/PINK to PINK: pink has less top end than white, so it sounds deeper and more natural, like wind or surf.
- MODE MONO: one voice for a single sound.
- Listen for: hold a key and hear a steady hiss. Every key sounds the same, since noise has no pitch. Flip to WHITE to hear it get brighter and thinner.

steps.title: Resonant filter with a slow contour
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. With emphasis it rings at the cutoff and gives the noise a hint of pitch. A slow contour (Moog’s word for envelope) brightens each wave as it rises.
- CUTOFF −1.5 (about 220 Hz): dark, a low roar.
- EMPHASIS 5: Moog’s word for resonance. Here it is how whistly the surf is: lower for rain, higher for wind.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 4: how bright each wave gets at its crest.
- ATTACK 1.4 s, DECAY 1.6 s, SUSTAIN 3: the filter takes over a second to open, then falls back.
- Listen for: hold a key. The roar brightens over a second or so, then settles darker. Sweep EMPHASIS to hear the whistle come in.

steps.title: Slow swell
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. Long times let each held key swell and break like a wave.
- ATTACK 1.4 s: each wave fades in slowly.
- DECAY 2.2 s, SUSTAIN 6: after the peak it falls back to a lower level, the wave breaking.
- DECAY switch on: with it on, DECAY is also the fade after you let go, so each wave washes out over about two seconds.
- Listen for: hold a key for a few seconds, then let go. Swell, break, then a long wash out.

steps.title: Chorus
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS II: the faster, deeper sweep. On noise it adds slow swirling movement and width.
- Listen for: on headphones, the surf moves around rather than sitting in the middle. Switch the chorus off to hear it collapse to a flat centre.

sounds.name: Rubber Funk Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Parliament — "Flash Light"
sounds.blurb: Round, fat bass with a quick "wow" on the front of every note.
sounds.how: The Minimoog bass, played in MONO so three oscillators stack on each note: two sawtooths a hair apart and one an octave down. The filter starts almost closed and a fast contour flicks it open and shut on each note, which is the rubbery "bow".

steps.title: Three stacked sawtooths
steps.why:
MONO stacks three oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone) on the one note: two saws a hair apart and one an octave down. This is the Minimoog bass layout, in the style of P-Funk.
- MODE MONO: every switched-on oscillator plays the key you press. In POLY each note would get only one of them.
- RANGE 16’ / 16’ / 32’: footage comes from organ pipes; 16’ is an octave below normal pitch, 32’ two octaves, for weight.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all three: the buzziest wave, plenty for the filter to sweep through.
- Osc 2 FREQUENCY +0.1: a tenth of a semitone sharp, so the two 16’ saws beat and the note moves.
- OSC 1–3 on, VOLUME 8 / 7.5 / 6.5: OSC 4 off. The 16’ saws lead and the sub sits a little lower.
- Listen for: hold a low note. Switch osc 3 off and on to hear the sub drop out and return.

steps.title: Close the filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Here it is pulled almost shut, which sets the dull thump between notes before the next step flicks it open.
- CUTOFF −2.6 (about 105 Hz): very low, so only the round bottom of the note is left.
- EMPHASIS 3.2: Moog’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. It will make the coming sweep vocal.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 on: a third of key tracking, so higher notes are not duller than low ones.
- Listen for: a muffled thump. That is expected for now.

steps.title: Flick it open
steps.why:
The filter contour is an envelope (Moog calls envelopes contours): each note pushes the cutoff up and lets it fall back. That quick flick open and shut is the rubbery “bow”.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 5.6: the size of the “wow”. Lower is a smoother bass; higher a harder quack.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): the filter opens at once, on the beat.
- DECAY 250 ms: the length of the “wow”. Around 200 ms sounds funky; longer becomes a slow sweep.
- SUSTAIN 1.5: held notes settle back to nearly closed.
- Listen for: every note now says “bow”. Sweep DECAY while the line plays to hear the groove change.

steps.title: Tight loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes volume over time, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. Funk bass wants a hard start and a clean stop.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): full level at once, lined up with the filter flick.
- SUSTAIN 8: held notes keep most of their weight.
- DECAY 220 ms with the DECAY switch on: the switch makes DECAY the fade after you let go. Short, so the gaps in the groove stay clean.
- Listen for: the space between notes. Switch DECAY off and notes stop dead, even tighter and more staccato.

sounds.name: Buzzing Saw Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Tubeway Army — "Are ‘Friends’ Electric?"
sounds.blurb: A wide-open, buzzing sawtooth lead that drones rather than sings.
sounds.how: Two sawtooths in MONO, detuned so they beat slowly, through a filter left almost fully open. There is no contour movement: the sound is the raw buzz of the oscillators, held at full level.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, slowly beating
steps.why:
Two sawtooth oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone) stacked in MONO, tuned slightly apart so they waver against each other. That slow, uneasy beating is the character of this lead, in the style of Tubeway Army.
- MODE MONO: both oscillators play the one key you press.
- RANGE 8’ on both: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on both: the brightest, buzziest wave.
- Osc 2 FREQUENCY +0.2: a fifth of a semitone sharp. Closer to 0 the beating slows and steadies; further away it sounds sour.
- OSC 1 and 2 on, VOLUME 7 each: 3 and 4 off. Two equal saws, so the beating is as deep as it can be.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the tone waver a few times a second. Set osc 2 FREQUENCY to 0 and it goes still.

steps.title: Open filter, no sweep
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Here it is left nearly wide open and does not move, so you hear the raw buzz of the oscillators for the whole note.
- CUTOFF 2.5 (about 3.6 kHz): high, so almost all the buzz comes through.
- EMPHASIS 1: Moog’s word for resonance. Just a trace, no whistle.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 0: the contour (Moog’s word for envelope) does not move the filter, so the tone stays the same from start to end.
- Listen for: a bright, steady drone. Turn CUTOFF down to 0 to hear it go dull, then back up.

steps.title: Held at full level
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. This lead drones, so it holds full level for as long as you hold the key.
- ATTACK 0.3 (2 ms): immediate, without a click.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level while held.
- DECAY 350 ms with the DECAY switch on: the switch makes DECAY the fade after you let go. A short tail, so the line stays tidy.
- Listen for: long notes that do not fade at all while held, then a short fade on release.

sounds.name: Round Staccato Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Kraftwerk — "Autobahn"
sounds.blurb: A short, round, bouncing bass with no bite at all.
sounds.how: Triangle and square in MONO give a soft, hollow tone with a strong fundamental. The filter is kept low with no emphasis, and short notes with no sustain make the line bounce.

steps.title: Triangle and square
steps.why:
MONO stacks a triangle and a square on one note: both soft, hollow waves with a strong fundamental (the note itself rather than its overtones). No bite, just a round, bouncing bass in the style of Kraftwerk.
- MODE MONO: both oscillators play the one key.
- Osc 1 RANGE 16’, triangle: footage comes from organ pipes; 16’ is an octave below normal pitch. Triangle is the softest wave, nearly a pure tone.
- Osc 2 RANGE 32’, square, FREQUENCY 0: a hollow square an octave further down gives the note its body.
- OSC 1 and 2 on, VOLUME 8 / 5.5: 3 and 4 off. The triangle leads and the square fills in under it.
- Listen for: switch osc 2 off and on while holding a note. Without it the bass is thin and flute-like; with it, it has body.

steps.title: Low, gentle filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. It is kept low with no emphasis, and a little contour (Moog’s word for envelope) softens the start of each note.
- CUTOFF −1.5 (about 220 Hz): low, so the square’s upper harmonics are rolled off.
- EMPHASIS 0: Moog’s word for resonance, turned off, so there is no squelch or edge.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 2.5, DECAY 280 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 2, a small lift at the start of each note that fades fast.
- Listen for: a round “bup” on each note. Raise EMPHASIS to 5 to hear what this sound is deliberately avoiding.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. With no sustain every note dies away on its own, which makes the line bounce.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant start.
- DECAY 330 ms, SUSTAIN 0: the length of each note. It falls to silence in about a third of a second, however long you hold.
- DECAY switch off: let go early and the note stops dead, so every note is equally short.
- Listen for: a bouncing staccato line. Sweep DECAY to lengthen or shorten every note at once.

sounds.name: Slow String Chords
sounds.ref: In the style of late-70s string-machine pads
sounds.blurb: Soft, slow chords with the chorus turning them into an ensemble.
sounds.how: Four sawtooths in POLY, a filter set bright but not harsh, and slow contours. The chorus with both buttons pressed gives the fast, shallow shimmer of the string machines of the time, which turns four single oscillators into something like a section.

steps.title: Four matching sawtooths
steps.why:
POLY gives each key you hold one of the four oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone), so a four-note chord uses them all. For a string section in the style of late-70s string machines, they must all match.
- MODE POLY: each new key takes the next oscillator in turn.
- RANGE 8’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all four: bright and full of harmonics, the nearest wave to a bowed string.
- FREQUENCY 0 on 2–4: in tune. The chorus will add the ensemble movement.
- OSC 1–4 on, VOLUME 5.5 each: every note of the chord present and even, at a moderate level so the filter is not driven hard.
- Listen for: hold a chord. Plain and bright for now.

steps.title: Bright but soft filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Here it is fairly open for brightness, with a small, slow contour (Moog’s word for envelope) and full key tracking.
- CUTOFF 0.8 (about 1.1 kHz): bright but not harsh.
- EMPHASIS 1: Moog’s word for resonance. Just a trace.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 1.5, ATTACK 770 ms: with DECAY 1.0 s and SUSTAIN 7, a gentle brightening as each chord comes in, then it settles almost where it peaked.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 and 2 on: full tracking, so the cutoff follows the notes and high chords are as bright as low ones.
- Listen for: play a chord low, then high. The colour stays the same across the keyboard.

steps.title: Slow in, slow out
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. Bowed strings take time to speak and to die away.
- ATTACK 4.4 (660 ms): the slow start of each chord, like a bow getting the strings going.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level while held.
- DECAY 1.0 s with the DECAY switch on: the switch makes DECAY the fade after you let go, so chords overlap as you change them.
- Listen for: chords that fade in over about two-thirds of a second and tail off for a second after release.

steps.title: Both chorus buttons
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which thickens it and spreads it across the two outputs. With both buttons pressed it gives the fast, shallow shimmer of string machines, which turns four single oscillators into something like a section.
- Chorus ON: puts the chorus in.
- CHORUS I and II together: a quick, shallow shimmer. Release II for a slower, deeper sweep.
- Listen for: switch the chorus off and on while holding a chord. On, it shimmers and widens like an ensemble; off, it is four plain oscillators.

sounds.name: Combo Organ
sounds.ref: In the style of 60s combo organ
sounds.blurb: Hollow square-wave chords that start and stop like an organ.
sounds.how: Squares in POLY, a steady filter and a loudness contour that is fully on while a key is down and off the instant it is released. AUTO DAMP matters here: with it on, each finger you lift stops its note, as on an organ.

steps.title: Four squares
steps.why:
POLY gives each key you hold one of the four oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone), so chords of up to four notes play. Squares have only odd harmonics: the hollow sound of a cheap 60s combo organ.
- MODE POLY: each new key takes the next oscillator.
- RANGE 8’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- WAVEFORM square on all four: hollow and reedy.
- FREQUENCY 0 on 2–4: exactly in tune, as an organ is.
- OSC 1–4 on, VOLUME 6 each: every note of a chord present and even.
- Listen for: hold a chord. Hollow and buzzy. Flip one WAVEFORM to sawtooth and one note turns brassier.

steps.title: Damp let-go notes
steps.why:
AUTO DAMP decides what happens to a note you let go while other keys are still held. It exists because all the notes share one loudness contour, which cannot release them one at a time.
- AUTO DAMP on: a key you lift stops its note at once, even while others are held, as on an organ. Off, lifted notes keep sounding until you let go of everything or play a new note.
- Listen for: hold a chord and lift one finger. That note stops. Switch AUTO DAMP off and try again: it rings on.

steps.title: Steady filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. An organ does not change colour during a note, so the filter is set once and left still.
- CUTOFF 1 (about 1.3 kHz): open enough for a bright, clear tone, while taking the sharpest edge off the squares.
- EMPHASIS 0: Moog’s word for resonance, off, so no whistle or squelch.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 0: the contour (Moog’s word for envelope) does not move the filter. A fixed tone.
- Listen for: the tone is the same from start to end of every chord.

steps.title: On-off loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. An organ is fully on while a key is down and off the instant it is released.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant start.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level for as long as you hold.
- DECAY 350 ms: with sustain at full it has nothing to do while you hold.
- DECAY switch off: the chord stops dead when you let go, with no fade.
- Listen for: chords that start and stop exactly with your fingers. Switch DECAY on to hear a short tail appear.

steps.title: A little chorus
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which thickens it and spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS II: the faster, deeper sweep. On an organ it gives a rough version of the wobble of a rotating speaker.
- Listen for: the chord starts to wobble and swirl. Try CHORUS I instead for a gentler, slower movement.

sounds.name: Plucked Chords
sounds.ref: In the style of 80s synth-pop plucked chords
sounds.blurb: Short, bright chord plucks that ring out and fade.
sounds.how: Four sawtooths in POLY with a fast filter contour and no sustain: each chord starts bright and falls away quickly. Because all four notes share one contour, every note of the chord plucks together.

steps.title: Four sawtooths
steps.why:
POLY gives each key you hold one of the four oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone). Matching oscillators give matching notes, so a chord sounds even.
- MODE POLY: each new key takes the next oscillator in turn, up to four.
- RANGE 8’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all four: bright and buzzy, which the filter will turn into a pluck.
- FREQUENCY +0.1 / −0.1 / 0 on 2–4: tiny offsets, so the chord is not perfectly clean.
- OSC 1–4 on, VOLUME 6 each: every note present and equally loud.
- Listen for: hold a chord. Bright and steady for now.

steps.title: Fast filter pluck
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. A fast contour (Moog’s word for envelope) opens it at once and closes it in a fraction of a second: the pluck. All four notes share it, so every note of a chord plucks together.
- CUTOFF −1.8 (about 180 Hz): dark at rest.
- EMPHASIS 2: Moog’s word for resonance. A little edge on each pluck.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 6: a big lift, so the pluck starts bright.
- ATTACK 1 ms, DECAY 280 ms, SUSTAIN 0: DECAY is how long the bright part lasts. It closes fully, even on held chords.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 on: a third of key tracking, so high chords stay a little brighter.
- Listen for: a bright “plink” that turns dull. Sweep DECAY to lengthen or shorten it.

steps.title: Ringing loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. With no sustain each chord rings out and fades on its own.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant, lined up with the filter pluck.
- DECAY 540 ms, SUSTAIN 0: how long each chord rings, about half a second, then silence even if held.
- DECAY switch on: let go early and the chord still rings out over the DECAY time instead of stopping.
- Listen for: short chords that fade. Raise DECAY for a longer ring, like a harp.

steps.title: Chorus I
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which thickens it and spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS I: the slow, gentle sweep. It widens the plucks without a wobble.
- Listen for: the plucks spread to both sides. Switch the chorus off to hear them narrow.

sounds.name: Driven Acid Line
sounds.ref: In the style of late-80s acid house
sounds.blurb: One sawtooth, high emphasis, glide and the distortion switched in.
sounds.how: A single sawtooth in MONO through the ladder filter with the emphasis high. A short contour makes every note squelch, glide slides into every note, and the distortion after the amplifier adds the grit acid lines usually get from a mixing desk pushed too hard.

steps.title: One sawtooth
steps.why:
A single sawtooth, the classic acid starting point: one bright, buzzy oscillator (the part that makes the raw tone) for the filter to squelch. MONO keeps it to one note at a time.
- MODE MONO: one note at a time.
- Osc 1 RANGE 16’: footage comes from organ pipes; 16’ is an octave below normal pitch, bass range.
- Osc 1 WAVEFORM sawtooth: full of harmonics, so the resonant filter has plenty to pick out.
- OSC 1 on, 2–4 off; VOLUME 8: one strong oscillator, and nothing else.
- Listen for: a plain, bright buzz. The squelch comes next.

steps.title: Resonant filter and a short contour
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. High emphasis and a short contour (Moog’s word for envelope) turn each opening into a squelch.
- CUTOFF −2.2 (about 140 Hz): low at rest. Turn it while the riff plays, as acid players do.
- EMPHASIS 7.6: Moog’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. High, so the filter sings as it moves. Below 5 it is just a bass.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 5: how far each note flicks the cutoff up.
- ATTACK 1 ms, DECAY 260 ms, SUSTAIN 0.5: open at once, close fast, settle almost shut.
- Listen for: a rubbery “yow” on every note. Sweep CUTOFF and DECAY while the riff plays.

steps.title: Glide
steps.why:
Glide slides the pitch from one note to the next instead of jumping. Here it slides into every note, whether or not the notes overlap. On the Poly D it has an on/off switch beside the keys and a time knob on the main panel.
- GLIDE switch on: without it the knob does nothing.
- GLIDE knob 2.2 (about 100 ms): short, a quick slur rather than a long swoop.
- Listen for: the pitch bending between notes. Switch GLIDE off and back on to hear the slides go and return.

steps.title: Loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. Here it just holds the level so the filter does all the shaping.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant start.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level while held, so the squelch is always heard.
- DECAY 280 ms with the DECAY switch on: a short fade after you let go.
- Listen for: notes stay at full volume while the tone squelches. Shape comes from the filter, not the volume.

steps.title: Grit
steps.why:
The distortion sits after the amplifier and before the chorus. It adds the grit acid lines usually got from a mixing desk pushed too hard.
- Distortion ON: puts it in the signal path.
- DIST 4: moderate drive. At 0 the line is clean and rounder; higher, it gets fuzzier and more compressed.
- TONE 6.5: bright, so the squelch cuts through. Left is smoother and darker.
- LEVEL 4: a little down, as the drive makes it louder.
- Listen for: switch the distortion off and on while the riff plays. On, the squelch is harder and grittier.

sounds.name: Clean Sub Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of modern pop and hip-hop sub bass
sounds.blurb: An almost pure low tone, felt as much as heard.
sounds.how: One triangle at 32’ with the filter low enough to take off what few harmonics it has. Glide lets notes slide, which sub-bass lines use a lot.

steps.title: One triangle, low
steps.why:
One low triangle, the softest wave here and almost a pure tone. A sub bass is felt as much as heard, in the style of modern pop and hip-hop.
- MODE MONO: one note at a time.
- Osc 1 RANGE 32’: footage comes from organ pipes; 32’ is two octaves under the normal 8’.
- Osc 1 WAVEFORM triangle: very few harmonics, so it is round and smooth.
- OSC 1 on, 2–4 off; VOLUME 8.5: one oscillator, strong.
- Listen for: a low, soft tone. On small speakers it may be hard to hear; headphones help.

steps.title: Filter low
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Here it rounds off the few harmonics the triangle has, so only the fundamental (the note itself) is left.
- CUTOFF −2.5 (about 110 Hz): low, taking off the upper harmonics.
- EMPHASIS 0: Moog’s word for resonance, off. A peak here would make the sub uneven from note to note.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 0: the contour (Moog’s word for envelope) does not move the filter, so the tone does not change.
- Listen for: even smoother than before. Turn CUTOFF up to 2 to hear the soft harmonics come back.

steps.title: Slides
steps.why:
Glide slides the pitch from one note to the next instead of jumping, something sub-bass lines use a lot. On the Poly D it has an on/off switch beside the keys and a time knob on the main panel.
- GLIDE switch on: without it the knob does nothing.
- GLIDE knob 3 (180 ms): a medium slide, clear but not lazy.
- Listen for: play a low note then one an octave up. The sub slides up between them.

steps.title: Smooth loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. A sub needs full, steady level and clean edges.
- ATTACK 0.7 (6 ms): a touch of fade-in, which stops the low note clicking as it starts.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level while held.
- DECAY 460 ms with the DECAY switch on: the switch makes DECAY the fade after you let go.
- Listen for: set ATTACK to 0 and hear a small click at the start of each note. Back to 0.7 and it is gone.

context.filter.cutoff: In this sound: low, so only the fundamental is left.

tweaks.hear: Harmonics come back, so the bass is heard on small speakers.
A hollower, more present sub.

sounds.name: Unison Rave Stab
sounds.ref: In the style of early-90s rave stabs
sounds.blurb: Four detuned oscillators on each note, chorused and driven.
sounds.how: UNI stacks all four oscillators on one key, each tuned a little apart, with Oscillator 4 an octave down. Chorus II makes the stack swirl and the distortion hardens it. Short stabs keep it punchy.

steps.title: Stack four on one key
steps.why:
UNI (unison) shares the four oscillators among the keys held, so one key gets all four. Each is tuned a little apart and the fourth drops an octave: a thick, swirling rave stack.
- MODE UNI: hold two keys and each gets two oscillators, so the stack thins out.
- RANGE 8’ on 1–3, 16’ on osc 4: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch, 16’ an octave down for weight.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all four: bright and buzzy.
- FREQUENCY +0.3 / −0.2 / +0.1 on 2–4: three different offsets, so the stack beats and swirls.
- OSC 1–4 on, VOLUME 6.5 / 6.5 / 6.5 / 6: all in, the low octave a little quieter.
- Listen for: hold one key. Wide and churning. Hold two and each note gets thinner.

steps.title: Open filter with a snap
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. It is fairly open, with a short contour (Moog’s word for envelope) that snaps it wider on each hit.
- CUTOFF 0.5 (about 890 Hz): bright enough for the stab to cut through a mix.
- EMPHASIS 2: Moog’s word for resonance. A little edge.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 3.5, DECAY 260 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 3, a quick snap of extra brightness at the front of each stab.
- Listen for: a bright hit at the start of each note that settles slightly.

steps.title: Stab loudness
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. Short and punchy keeps stabs from clogging the mix.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant, for punch.
- DECAY 350 ms, SUSTAIN 4: after the hit it drops to under half level, so even held stabs sound short.
- DECAY switch on: a short fade after release rather than a dead stop.
- Listen for: a loud front then a quieter tail while you hold.

steps.title: Chorus II and distortion
steps.why:
The chorus and distortion both sit after the amplifier: distortion first, then chorus. Chorus II makes the stack swirl and the distortion hardens it.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS II: the faster, deeper sweep, which adds more swirl to the already detuned stack.
- Distortion ON, DIST 3.5: moderate drive, which compresses and hardens the stab.
- TONE 6: a little bright, so it cuts.
- LEVEL 4.5: slightly down to match the level without it.
- Listen for: switch the distortion off and on. On, the stab is harder and denser. Then try the chorus off to hear the swirl drop away.

sounds.name: Thin Reed Lead
sounds.ref: The high-pass filter mode used for a lead
sounds.blurb: A nasal lead with the bass taken away by the high-pass filter.
sounds.how: The FILTER MODE switch set to HI turns the ladder filter into a high-pass: it takes away the low part of the sound instead of the top. With a narrow pulse and some emphasis at the cutoff, what is left is thin and reedy, like an oboe played through a small speaker.

steps.title: A narrow pulse
steps.why:
A narrow pulse is the thinnest, most nasal wave on the Poly D, a good start for a reedy lead. MONO keeps it to one note at a time.
- MODE MONO: one note at a time.
- Osc 1 RANGE 8’: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- Osc 1 WAVEFORM narrow pulse: thin and nasal. There is no pulse-width knob, so this is one of three fixed widths.
- OSC 1 on, 2–4 off; VOLUME 7.5: a single oscillator.
- Listen for: a buzzy, nasal tone, already thin before the filter.

steps.title: High-pass
steps.why:
FILTER MODE HI turns the ladder filter into a high-pass: it takes away the low part of the sound instead of the top. With some emphasis at the cutoff, what is left is thin and reedy, like an oboe through a small speaker.
- FILTER MODE HI: high-pass. It is Behringer’s addition; the Minimoog filter is low-pass only.
- CUTOFF 0.5 (about 890 Hz): everything below here is cut. Higher means thinner.
- EMPHASIS 4: Moog’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Gives the reedy peak.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 0: no filter movement.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 and 2 on: full tracking, so the peak stays at the same place relative to each note.
- Listen for: flip FILTER MODE to LO and the same settings give a round, dark lead. Back to HI.

steps.title: Glide and sustain
steps.why:
Glide slides the pitch between notes, and the loudness contour (the volume shape, the job a VCA, or voltage-controlled amplifier, does on other synths) holds each note at full level, like a wind player.
- GLIDE switch on, knob 2 (80 ms): a small scoop into each note.
- Loudness ATTACK 0.5 (4 ms): a soft, quick start.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level while held.
- DECAY 460 ms with the DECAY switch on: the fade after you let go.
- Listen for: play a slow melody. Notes scoop slightly into pitch and hold steady.

sounds.name: Noise Snare
sounds.ref: In the style of early drum-machine snares
sounds.blurb: A short burst of filtered white noise with a tone under it.
sounds.how: White noise gives the rattle, a triangle an octave up the body of the drum. Both contours are short with no sustain, so each hit is a snap however long the key is held.

steps.title: Noise and a tone
steps.why:
A snare is two things: the rattle of the snares and the tone of the drum. White noise gives the rattle and a triangle gives the body.
- MODE MONO: one hit at a time.
- Noise ON, NOISE VOLUME 8, WHITE: white noise is bright and hissy, like snare wires.
- Osc 1 RANGE 4’, triangle: footage comes from organ pipes; 4’ is an octave above normal pitch. A soft tone for the drum body.
- OSC 1 on, VOLUME 5; OSC 2–4 off: the body sits under the rattle. Raise it for a more tom-like snare.
- Listen for: a steady hiss with a faint tone under it. The contours will turn it into a hit.

steps.title: Bright filter snap
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. A very short contour (Moog’s word for envelope) opens it wide for an instant, so each hit has a bright crack.
- CUTOFF 0.5 (about 890 Hz): the noise is dulled at rest.
- EMPHASIS 1: Moog’s word for resonance. Barely there.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 4, DECAY 140 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 0, a flash of brightness that closes fully in about a seventh of a second.
- Listen for: a bright crack at the front of each hit, then duller hiss.

steps.title: Short hit
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. For a drum the hit must die away by itself, however long the key is held.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant.
- DECAY 250 ms, SUSTAIN 0: the length of the hit, a quarter of a second, then silence.
- DECAY switch on: the tail is the same whether you hold the key or let go early.
- Listen for: tap and hold. Both give the same short snap. Sweep DECAY for a tighter or longer snare.

sounds.name: Feedback Growl
sounds.ref: The Minimoog feedback trick
sounds.blurb: A thick, overdriven bass made by feeding the output back into the mixer.
sounds.how: Minimoog players ran a cable from the output back into the external input to overdrive the mixer and filter. In this app the EXT IN channel does that with no cable: switch it on and raise its volume, and the sound goes round the loop and thickens.

steps.title: Three hot oscillators
steps.why:
MONO stacks three loud oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone) on one note. Hot levels matter here: the feedback loop in the next step works on whatever goes into the mixer.
- MODE MONO: every switched-on oscillator plays the key you press.
- RANGE 16’ / 16’ / 32’: footage comes from organ pipes; 16’ is an octave below normal pitch, 32’ two octaves, for weight.
- WAVEFORM saw / saw / square: two buzzy saws with a hollow square underneath.
- Osc 2 FREQUENCY −0.1: a tenth of a semitone flat, so the two saws beat and the note moves.
- OSC 1–3 on, VOLUME 8.5 / 8.5 / 7.5: OSC 4 off. All high, so the filter is already driven a little.
- Listen for: a thick, slightly rough bass before any feedback.

steps.title: Switch in the feedback
steps.why:
Minimoog players ran a cable from the output back into the external input to overdrive the mixer and filter. In this app the EXT IN (external input) channel does that with no cable: the synth’s own output is fed back into the mixer.
- EXT IN on: connects the feedback path.
- EXT IN VOLUME 6: the feedback amount. Below 4 it thickens; above 7 it breaks up.
- Output VOLUME 7: the volume is inside the loop, so it changes the distortion as well as the level.
- Listen for: watch the OVERLOAD lamp as you play. Sweep EXT IN VOLUME from 0 to 8 to hear clean turn to growl.

steps.title: Filter part open
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. It is opened part way, so the grit from the loop comes through, and a medium contour (Moog’s word for envelope) adds a lift on each note.
- CUTOFF −1.2 (about 280 Hz): dark, but enough brightness for the growl to be heard.
- EMPHASIS 2.5: Moog’s word for resonance. A little edge; inside a feedback loop more can howl.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 4.2, DECAY 600 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 3.5, each note starts brighter and grittier, then settles.
- Listen for: a snarl at the front of each note that eases back as you hold.

steps.title: Full sustain
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. Full sustain keeps the level, and so the distortion, even while notes are held.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant start.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level while held, so the loop stays driven.
- DECAY 350 ms: with the DECAY switch still on from the start, this is also the short fade after you let go.
- Listen for: long notes keep growling at the same intensity. Lower SUSTAIN and the growl fades with the level.

context.mix.ext: In this sound: the feedback amount. Below 4 it thickens; above 7 it breaks up.

The bass goes and only the snarling top is left.

sounds.name: Latched Arpeggio Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Italo-disco octave basses
sounds.blurb: Hold one chord and the arpeggiator runs a two-octave bass line on its own.
sounds.how: The arpeggiator in its two-octave UP order climbs through the held notes and then repeats them an octave higher. HOLD keeps it running after you let go. Short, plucky contours keep every step separate.

steps.title: A punchy bass voice
steps.why:
A punchy bass voice for the arpeggiator to play: a sawtooth with a square an octave under it, stacked in MONO so every arpeggio step gets both.
- MODE MONO: both oscillators play each note.
- Osc 1 RANGE 16’, sawtooth: footage comes from organ pipes; 16’ is an octave below normal pitch. The bright part.
- Osc 2 RANGE 32’, square, FREQUENCY 0: an octave further down and in tune, for weight.
- OSC 1 and 2 on, VOLUME 7.5 / 6: 3 and 4 off. The saw leads.
- Listen for: a solid, buzzy bass note. Switch osc 2 off and on to hear the weight under it.

steps.title: Blip contours
steps.why:
Short filter and loudness contours (Moog’s word for envelopes) make every arpeggio step a separate blip. The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs.
- CUTOFF −2 (about 160 Hz), EMPHASIS 3.5: dark at rest, with some resonance (Moog calls it emphasis) for a little quack.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 5, DECAY 240 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 0, a bright pop at the start of each note that closes fully.
- Loudness DECAY 280 ms, SUSTAIN 0: with ATTACK at 1 ms, each note dies away on its own.
- DECAY switch off: notes stop dead when released.
- Listen for: tap a note and hear a short, snappy blip.

steps.title: Arpeggiator, two octaves up, latched
steps.why:
The arpeggiator plays the keys you hold one after another, as sixteenth notes at the TEMPO rate. UP 2 OCT climbs the held notes, then repeats them an octave higher: the Italo-disco octave bass.
- ARP on: starts it.
- STEP UP 2 OCT: two held notes become a four-step line. The LOCATION lamps show the chosen order.
- HOLD on: keeps the line going after you let go. A new chord replaces the old one.
- TEMPO 5 (98 BPM): the speed of the line.
- Listen for: hold one low note, let go and the octave line keeps running. Add a second note to hear it become four steps.

context.arp.order: In this sound: UP 2 OCT, so two held notes become a four-step line.
context.arp.hold: In this sound: keeps the line going after you let go.

tweaks.hear: A faster, more frantic line.

sounds.name: Glass Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of 80s bell-like synth keys
sounds.blurb: Bright, glassy chords that ring and fade like struck glass.
sounds.how: Triangles an octave up (4’) are close to pure tones, and a resonant filter with a quick contour adds a glassy click at the start. No sustain and a long decay let each chord ring away, and the chorus gives it shimmer.

steps.title: High triangles
steps.why:
Triangles up an octave are close to pure tones, the base of a glassy, bell-like keys sound. POLY gives each key its own oscillator, so chords play.
- MODE POLY: each new key takes the next oscillator in turn.
- RANGE 4’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 4’ is an octave above normal 8’ pitch, high and clear.
- WAVEFORM triangle on all four: soft, few harmonics.
- FREQUENCY 0 on 2–4: in tune, so chords are clean and bell-like.
- OSC 1–4 on, VOLUME 7 each: triangles are quiet, so a higher level.
- Listen for: soft, flute-like chords for now.

steps.title: Glassy click
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. With high emphasis, a quick contour (Moog’s word for envelope) makes the resonant peak ping across the notes at the start of each chord: the glassy click.
- CUTOFF 0 (about 630 Hz): a middle position.
- EMPHASIS 6: Moog’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. High enough to ring, which is the ping.
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 4, DECAY 250 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 1, a fast sweep down at the start of each chord.
- KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 and 2 on: full tracking, so the ping sits in the same place relative to each note.
- Listen for: a bright “tink” at the start. Turn EMPHASIS down to 2 and it goes.

steps.title: Ring out
steps.why:
The loudness contour shapes the volume, the job a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) does on other synths. For struck glass, the sound must ring and fade on its own.
- ATTACK 0 (1 ms): instant, like a strike.
- DECAY 900 ms, SUSTAIN 0: how long the chords ring, just under a second, even if held.
- DECAY switch on: let go early and it still rings out.
- Listen for: chords that ping and ring away. Raise DECAY for a longer, bell-like tail.

steps.title: Chorus I
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS I: the slow, gentle sweep. On bright tones it adds shimmer.
- Listen for: the ringing tails shimmer and widen. Switch the chorus off to hear them go plain and central.

context.aenv.decay: In this sound: how long the chords ring.

sounds.name: Chords over a Drone
sounds.ref: OSC 4 CONTROL off: a fixed drone under three-note chords
sounds.blurb: Oscillator 4 holds one low note while the other three play your chords above it.
sounds.how: With OSC 4 CONTROL off, Oscillator 4 ignores the keys and is left out of the POLY sharing, so the other three oscillators play up to three-note chords while Oscillator 4 sits on a fixed pitch underneath. Its FREQUENCY knob tunes the drone. It shares the filter and contours, so it swells with every chord.

steps.title: Three matching oscillators for the chords
steps.why:
Oscillators 1 to 3 will play the chords, so they are set the same. Oscillator 4 is saved for the drone in the next step.
- MODE POLY: each key you hold takes an oscillator of its own.
- RANGE 8’ on 1–3: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on 1–3: bright and full.
- FREQUENCY 0 on 2 and 3: in tune.
- OSC 1–4 on; VOLUME 5.5 on 1–3: even chord notes. Osc 4 stays in the mixer for the drone.
- Listen for: chords of up to four notes for now, since Oscillator 4 still follows the keys.

steps.title: Free Oscillator 4 from the keys
steps.why:
OSC 4 CONTROL off frees Oscillator 4 from the keys. It is left out of the POLY sharing and plays a fixed pitch, so the other three play up to three-note chords over it.
- OSC 4 CONTROL off: no key is ever given to Oscillator 4, and it ignores the keys and TUNE.
- RANGE 32’, triangle: footage comes from organ pipes; 32’ is two octaves below normal pitch. A soft, low tone.
- FREQUENCY 0.7: the pitch of the drone. With OSC 4 CONTROL off the knob covers a much wider range, so this small move retunes it by a few semitones.
- VOLUME 7: how loud the drone is under the chords.
- Listen for: it shares the filter and loudness contour, so the drone sounds only while keys are held. Play different chords and the low note stays put.

steps.title: A soft, swelling filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Slow contours (Moog’s word for envelopes) make each chord and the drone bloom together, since all four oscillators share them.
- CUTOFF −0.8 (about 360 Hz), EMPHASIS 1.5: soft, with a trace of resonance (Moog calls it emphasis).
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 3, ATTACK 680 ms: with DECAY 1.0 s and SUSTAIN 6, the filter opens gently over two-thirds of a second.
- Loudness ATTACK 540 ms, SUSTAIN 10: each chord fades in over half a second.
- Loudness DECAY 1.0 s, DECAY switch on: a second-long fade after you let go.
- Listen for: chord and drone swelling in together each time you play.

steps.title: Chorus
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS I: the slow, gentle sweep. It widens the chords and gives the static drone some movement.
- Listen for: switch the chorus off and on. On, the drone and chords spread out to both sides.

sounds.name: Hanging Chords
sounds.ref: AUTO DAMP off: let-go notes ring on
sounds.blurb: Lift fingers one at a time and the chord stays whole until the next new note.
sounds.how: With AUTO DAMP off, a note you let go keeps sounding for as long as any key is held, and stops only when you play a new note. So you can strike a chord, lift all but one finger and still hear the whole chord, then play a melody note to clear it. The phrase does exactly that.

steps.title: Four matching oscillators
steps.why:
POLY gives each key you hold one of the four oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone). Squares give a mellow, hollow tone, something like an electric piano.
- MODE POLY: each new key takes the next oscillator in turn.
- RANGE 8’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- WAVEFORM square on all four: hollow and soft-edged.
- FREQUENCY +0.1 on osc 2, 0 on 3 and 4: a hair of movement on one note.
- OSC 1–4 on, VOLUME 6 each: every chord note present and even.
- Listen for: hollow, steady chords.

steps.title: AUTO DAMP off
steps.why:
AUTO DAMP decides what happens to a note you let go while other keys are held. It exists because the notes share one loudness contour, which cannot release them one at a time.
- AUTO DAMP off: a note you let go keeps sounding as long as any key is held, and stops only when you play a new note. Switch it on and only the held notes continue.
- Listen for: strike a chord, lift all but the bass key and the whole chord hangs on. Play a new melody note to clear it.

steps.title: A plucked-then-held shape
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. A quick contour (Moog’s word for envelope) gives each chord a bright start that settles into a held tone.
- CUTOFF −1 (about 320 Hz), EMPHASIS 1: warm, with a trace of resonance (Moog calls it emphasis).
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 4, DECAY 600 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 3, bright at the start, then settles darker.
- Loudness DECAY 770 ms, SUSTAIN 7: with ATTACK at 1 ms, a key-like hit that settles to a held level.
- DECAY switch on: a fade after you let go.
- Listen for: each chord plucks then holds. The hanging notes stay at the held level.

steps.title: Chorus II
steps.why:
The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which thickens it and spreads it across the two outputs.
- Chorus ON with CHORUS II: the faster, deeper sweep. It suits a keyboard sound, like the chorus on an electric piano.
- Listen for: the held chords wobble and widen. Try CHORUS I instead for a slower, gentler movement.

sounds.name: Unison Duo Lead
sounds.ref: UNI with two keys: two detuned oscillators each
sounds.blurb: Play in thirds and sixths: each of the two notes gets its own detuned pair.
sounds.how: In UNI the oscillators are dealt out among the keys held. One key gets all four; two keys get two each, so a two-note harmony line has a detuned pair on each note. Oscillators 1 and 3 take one note, 2 and 4 the other, so the small detune on 3 and 4 thickens both.

steps.title: Four sawtooths, two slightly detuned
steps.why:
In UNI (unison) the oscillators are dealt out among the keys held. One key gets all four; two keys get two each, so a two-note harmony line has a detuned pair on each note.
- MODE UNI: with two keys held, Oscillators 1 and 3 take one note, 2 and 4 the other.
- RANGE 8’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all four: bright, full lead tone.
- FREQUENCY 0 / +0.1 / −0.1 on 2–4: the offsets on 3 and 4 detune one oscillator of each pair, so both notes beat.
- OSC 1–4 on, VOLUME 6.5 each: even pairs.
- Listen for: play in thirds or sixths and watch the lamps pair up. Each note is thicker than a single oscillator.

steps.title: Singing filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. It is fairly open, with some emphasis for a singing edge and full key tracking.
- CUTOFF 0.3 (about 780 Hz): bright enough for a lead.
- EMPHASIS 3: Moog’s word for resonance. A vocal edge without whistle.

- GLIDE switch on, knob 2.5 (130 ms): a short slide.
- Loudness ATTACK 0.3 (2 ms): immediate, no click.
- SUSTAIN 10: full level while held.
- DECAY 600 ms with the DECAY switch on: the fade after you let go.

sounds.name: Spread Octave Chords
sounds.ref: POLY with two oscillators an octave down
sounds.blurb: Every other note of a chord drops an octave, so close chords play as wide voicings.
sounds.how: In POLY each note of a chord lands on the next oscillator. Setting Oscillators 2 and 4 an octave lower than 1 and 3 means the second and fourth notes of each chord drop down, which spreads a close chord shape into a wide one. steps.title: Alternate octaves
steps.why:
In POLY each note of a chord lands on the next oscillator. Setting Oscillators 2 and 4 an octave below 1 and 3 drops every other note of a chord, which spreads a close chord shape into a wide voicing. A fully polyphonic synth cannot do this.

- RANGE 8’ on 1 and 3, 16’ on 2 and 4: footage comes from organ pipes; 16’ is an octave below 8’. Second and fourth notes sound an octave down.

sounds.name: Rotating Arpeggio

sounds.blurb: Each arpeggio step lands on the next oscillator, so the line cycles through four colours.
sounds.how: The arpeggiator plays one note at a time, and in POLY each new note takes the next oscillator. With the four set differently, the arpeggio and the oscillator rotation run against each other: a three-note chord arpeggiated over four oscillators takes twelve steps to repeat its colours.

steps.title: Four different oscillators
steps.why:
The arpeggiator plays one note at a time, and in POLY each new note takes the next oscillator. Set the four differently and each step of the arpeggio has its own colour and octave.
- MODE POLY: moves each step to the next oscillator. In MONO every step would play all four at once.

- Osc 2 RANGE 4’, square: an octave up, hollow.
- Osc 3 RANGE 8’, triangle: soft.
- Osc 4 RANGE 16’, narrow pulse: an octave down, thin and nasal.

steps.title: Plucky shape

Short filter and loudness contours (Moog’s word for envelopes) make each step distinct. The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs.

- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 4.5, DECAY 260 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 1, a quick pop of brightness on each step.

- STEP UP: climbs through the held notes and starts again. Try RANDOM and the colours and notes shuffle independently.
- HOLD on: the line keeps going after you let go.

steps.title: High, pure oscillators
steps.why:
High, pure oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone) make a bell-like tone for the arpeggio. MONO stacks them all on each step.
- MODE MONO: every switched-on oscillator plays each note.
- Osc 1 RANGE 4’, triangle: footage comes from organ pipes; 4’ is an octave above normal pitch. The main soft tone.
- Osc 2 RANGE 2’, triangle, FREQUENCY 0: two octaves up, for sparkle.
- Osc 3 RANGE 4’, square: a little hollow edge.

steps.title: Bell shape
steps.why:
A bell shape: a quick filter blip and a ringing loudness decay with no sustain. The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder, set fairly open, and contour is Moog’s word for envelope.
- CUTOFF 1 (about 1.3 kHz), EMPHASIS 2: open, with a little resonance (Moog calls it emphasis).
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 2, DECAY 350 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 2, a small bright tick at each strike.
- Loudness DECAY 700 ms, SUSTAIN 0: with ATTACK at 1 ms, it rings and fades, even if held. The loudness contour does the job of a VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) on other synths.
- DECAY switch on: the ring carries on after release.

steps.title: Two-octave arpeggio

The arpeggiator plays the keys you hold one after another, as sixteenth notes at the TEMPO rate. UP/DOWN 2 OCT runs the chord up over two octaves and back down.
- ARP on: starts it.
- STEP UP/DOWN 2 OCT: the held notes, then the same an octave higher, and back. The LOCATION lamps show the order.
- TEMPO 5.6 (109 BPM): a lively speed.

steps.title: Both chorus buttons

The chorus mixes in delayed copies of the sound with the delay swept up and down, which spreads it across the two outputs. With both buttons pressed it gives a fast, shallow shimmer.
- Chorus ON: puts it in.
- CHORUS I and II together: the fast shimmer that makes the arpeggio sparkle.

sounds.name: Distorted Chords
sounds.ref: Paraphonic chords through the distortion
sounds.blurb: Chords driven hard, so the notes grind against each other.
sounds.how: The distortion comes after the amplifier, so a whole chord goes into it at once. Distorting several notes together creates extra tones between them, the same reason guitarists play power chords rather than full chords through fuzz. Fifths and octaves stay clean-sounding; thirds turn gritty.

steps.title: Matching sawtooths
steps.why:
POLY gives each key you hold one of the four oscillators (the parts that make the raw tone), so chords of up to four notes play. Matching them means every note of a power chord has the same tone.
- MODE POLY: each new key takes the next oscillator in turn.
- RANGE 8’ on all four: footage comes from organ pipes; 8’ is normal pitch.
- WAVEFORM sawtooth on all four: bright and buzzy, good material for distortion.
- FREQUENCY 0 on 2–4: in tune, so fifths and octaves lock together cleanly.
- OSC 1–4 on, VOLUME 6 each: every note present and even.
- Listen for: clean, bright chords for now.

steps.title: Mid filter
steps.why:
The filter is a Moog-style low-pass ladder: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. Taking some top off before the distortion stops it fizzing. The loudness contour (the volume shape, the job a VCA, or voltage-controlled amplifier, does on other synths) keeps the chords held.
- CUTOFF −0.3 (about 510 Hz), EMPHASIS 1.5: a mid cutoff with a trace of resonance (Moog calls it emphasis).
- AMOUNT OF CONTOUR 2.5, DECAY 460 ms: with ATTACK at 1 ms and SUSTAIN 5, the contour (Moog’s word for envelope) adds a small lift at the start of each chord.
- Loudness DECAY 350 ms, SUSTAIN 9: with ATTACK at 1 ms, chords start at once and hold near full level.
- DECAY switch on: a short fade after you let go.
- Listen for: warmer, rounder chords with a slight push at the start.

steps.title: Drive the chords
steps.why:
The distortion sits after the amplifier, so the whole chord goes into it at once. Distorting several notes together creates extra tones between them, the reason guitarists play power chords rather than full chords through fuzz.
- Distortion ON: puts it in the signal path.
- DIST 7: driven hard, so the chord grinds.
- TONE 4: a little dark. Lower keeps the grind thick; higher makes it rasp.
- LEVEL 3: well down, as heavy drive makes it much louder.
- Listen for: play a fifth, then a major triad. The fifth stays solid and clean-sounding; the third makes the chord gritty and rough.
